planting.note: Divide offsets in spring into a mineral, fast-draining mix with the crown slightly above grade; withhold all water through summer dry-dormancy.

directions: One of the smallest Dudleyas, this species forms dense mats of narrow clavate leaves ideal for rock garden crevices, troughs, and bonsai-style succulent dishes where larger Dudleyas would overwhelm the scale. Because the rosettes stay so small, it disappears in competition with vigorous neighbors — pair it only with other dwarf succulents or bare gravel. Resume light watering only when fall rains would naturally begin.

planting.note: Plant divisions or seedlings in a crevice or slope with gravel mulch to keep the crown dry; give afternoon shade in low-desert heat.

directions: The most heat- and cold-tolerant Dudleya in general cultivation, native to desert mountain crevices from the Mojave and Sonoran region into Baja, this species fills the Dudleya-for-hot-dry-rockeries niche the mostly coastal and chaparral species already in cultivation don't cover. This is the Dudleya to use for inland or high-desert rock gardens where winter lows exceed what coastal species tolerate. Clusters slowly bulk up into multi-rosette mounds over several seasons rather than spreading by runners.

planting.note: Plant divisions or seed on a gentle slope in heavy clay soil, unamended with grit; source only nursery-propagated stock given its rarity.

directions: Unusual among Dudleyas for thriving in heavy clay rather than rock or gravel, this species is useful for native-plant gardeners whose site doesn't suit the typical crevice-garden Dudleyas, and is a valuable restoration and pollinator plant for Southern California clay-soil habitat gardens. Don't fix the soil with grit as you would for other succulents. Let it go fully dormant and leafless in summer heat without any irrigation, since it's rare and declining from development pressure in its native coastal plain habitat.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated offsets in a lean, rocky, fast-draining mix; never wild-collect, since this is a federally listed species restricted to three known occurrences.

directions: A federally threatened Conejo Mountain endemic restricted to volcanic rock outcrops, this is a genuinely rare species nonetheless available from native-plant specialty growers for collectors wanting to grow regionally significant, geologically specific succulents. Mimic its native volcanic substrate with a lean, rocky mix, avoiding rich potting soil, which encourages rot. Treat it as a conservation-value collector's plant rather than a mass-landscaping groundcover.

planting.note: Plant divisions or cuttings in the sunniest, most reflective rock-garden spot available; keep bone dry in summer dormancy, resuming water only with autumn cooling.

directions: Extending the genus's cultivated range further east and inland than any other species in the collection, native to Arizona, Nevada, and Utah desert mountains, this fills the true-desert, non-coastal Dudleya slot for xeric gardens outside coastal California. It comes from exposed desert canyon walls and tolerates more direct heat than the coastal Dudleyas already in cultivation. Red-orange spring flower spikes make it a useful accent against gray desert gravel.

planting.note: Plant nursery-grown stock on a rocky slope or raised bed with excellent drainage, away from foot traffic given the sticky leaf coating.

directions: One of only two Dudleyas with sticky, resin-scented foliage, this species offers a genuinely distinct textural and sensory feature among the genus, and the oily coating may deter some browsing insects, making it a conversation-piece succulent for a native collector's garden. Site on a rocky slope echoing its native Orange, San Diego, and Riverside County bluff habitat. Known from only about 20 wild occurrences, so treat it as a specialty conservation planting and buy only nursery-grown stock.

planting.note: Grow in full sun with no summer irrigation; source seed or plants only from reputable native nurseries given its CNPS rarity rank.

directions: A San Diego County and northern Baja mesa-top and vernal-pool-margin species, this Dudleya tolerates the seasonally saturated-then-baked-dry clay and hardpan conditions of San Diego mesa tops better than most rock-garden relatives, making it a good match for gardeners with heavier native soil who still want a true Dudleya rather than amending for a crevice species. It is a CNPS-listed rarity, giving it conservation-gardening value beyond its ornamental merit.
